fields.meta_title: Content Workflow: What It Is and How to Build One | Emergent
fields.meta_description: A content workflow is the set of steps and owners that carry each piece to publish. Follow one article through it, then build yours.
fields.h1: Build a Content Workflow That Carries Each Article to Publish
fields.hero_description: Build a content workflow that assigns each brief, flags late drafts, and sends finished articles to your CMS.
fields.features_heading: What the App Takes Off an Editor's Plate
fields.features_subheading: Every stage of the content workflow gets an owner and a date, on one board the whole marketing team reads.
fields.feature_1:
Briefs that arrive complete

The request form needs a topic, an audience, and a publish date before it accepts a brief. A routing rule written as a plain sentence picks the writer from the topic.
fields.feature_2:
Stage dates worked back from launch

Tell the app how many days drafting and editing take, and it counts back from the publish date to set each one. Push the launch out a week and both dates move with it.
fields.feature_3:
A nudge when a piece stalls

Each stage has an owner you name. If an item sits past its stage date, that owner gets a Slack message or an email linking to it, and a reminder follows a day later.
fields.feature_4:
Your CMS fed through its API

Emergent connects the app to any CMS with an API. Approved copy goes over with its SEO fields, and the post ID the CMS returns is stored next to the brief it came from.
fields.feature_5:
One board for the whole pipeline

Columns show each piece by stage and update the moment someone moves a card. Filter by writer before Monday planning to see which writers already have three pieces due.
fields.feature_6:
Records and code that stay yours

Every brief and its publish history live in a database you own. On paid plans, the full code of the app exports to your GitHub repository to read or change in any code editor.

fields.usecase_heading: One Article Through a Content Workflow
fields.tab_content_1:
Each brief leaves the form with a writer and due dates

Ines Valdivieso, a product marketer at Tallowpine, fills in a brief for How to forecast churn, written for finance leads, with a Nov 12 publish date. The app creates item C-114 on the content board and assigns it to Joaquin Ferreyra, who covers Forecasting. His draft is due Oct 29, counted back from the publish date.
fields.tab_content_2:
When a draft misses its date, the managing editor knows

Joaquin Ferreyra's draft was due Oct 29. On Oct 31, C-114 is still in Drafting, 2 days late. It is marked Late on the board. The managing editor, Halvard Brekke, gets a direct message with the brief plus an Open item button. From there he can set a new date or hand the piece to another writer.
fields.tab_content_3:
Finished articles reach the CMS with every field filled

Halvard Brekke reads the final edit of C-114 and marks it Ready. The app sends the article to the Tallowpine CMS through its API as a post scheduled for Nov 12 at 9:00 AM, with the title, slug, meta description, and author filled in. The CMS answers with a post ID, and the app saves it on C-114.
fields.tab_content_4:
Every live post opens repurposing tasks for the social lead

The churn article goes live on Nov 12. Mireille Kantor, who runs social and email, gets 3 repurposing tasks from the app: a newsletter summary due Nov 13 and 2 social posts due Nov 14. Each task links to the live post and stays on the board until Mireille marks it done.

fields.howto_title: How to Build a Content Workflow
fields.howto_description: Seven steps to map your content workflow, build it with Emergent, and test it on last month's articles before it runs live.
fields.howto_step_1_title: 01 List the stages and their owners
fields.howto_step_2_title: 02 Decide what a brief must hold
fields.howto_step_3_title: 03 Give each stage a length in days
fields.howto_step_4_title: 04 Name who hears about a late piece
fields.howto_step_1_des: List every stage a piece passes through on its way to readers, and the one person who owns each. Keep the names your team already uses, such as Drafting or Ready. The board should read the way people talk.
fields.howto_step_2_des: Pick the fields a request needs before writing starts, with the audience and the publish date at the top. A brief sent back for a missing audience costs a day; a draft written for the wrong reader costs a week.
fields.howto_step_3_des: Write down how long drafting and editing take for a standard post. Emergent builds the board and its date logic from a prompt that states those numbers in plain sentences.
fields.howto_step_4_des: Give each stage one person who gets the message when an item passes its date. Pick an editor by name, not a team channel, because an alert that reaches everyone has no owner.
fields.howto_step_5_title: 05 Connect the CMS and the alerts
fields.howto_step_5_des: Connect your CMS through its API so finished articles arrive as scheduled posts, and connect Slack or email for alerts. Map each board field to the CMS field it fills before the first send.
fields.howto_step_6_title: 06 Run last month's pieces through it
fields.howto_step_6_des: Send last month's pieces through the app before a live brief touches it. Check that every brief reached the right writer and that each date matches what happened last month. Fix a rule by prompting, then run the month again.
fields.howto_step_7_title: 07 Switch on one stage at a time
fields.howto_step_7_des: Start with brief intake, since it publishes nothing. After 2 weeks, compare missed dates with the 2 weeks before, then turn on the CMS handoff and, last, the repurposing tasks.

faq_plan.a: A content workflow is the series of tasks your team performs to take a piece of content through ideation and on to delivery, as HubSpot defines it. Each task has an owner and a due date. You can tell a working one by a simple test: anyone on the team can open the board and say who holds each piece and when it is due.

faq_plan.q: How do I create a content workflow?
faq_plan.a: Start by listing the stages your pieces pass through, then give each one an owner and a length in days. Begin with the stage that slips most often, since that is where a tracker pays back first. With Emergent's AI automation builder, you describe that setup in a prompt and get the brief form and the late-piece alerts as one app. You change it later by prompting again.

faq_plan.q: What is a good workflow for content creators?
faq_plan.ref: What is a good workflow for content creators?

prov.original: What is a good workflow for content creators?

faq_plan.a: A good workflow for content creators is one short enough to repeat every week. Batch the writing or filming into fixed blocks, and edit on another day. Publish on a set schedule, then run a content repurposing workflow that cuts each piece into smaller posts. A solo creator can build a tracker for that loop with Emergent and start free.

faq_plan.q: How do you integrate a digital content workflow into marketing processes?
faq_plan.ref: how do we integrate digital content workflows into marketing processes
faq_plan.a: Tie every piece to the campaign it serves, and let the campaign calendar set the publish dates. Record the campaign on each brief, and your reports can show which articles fed which launch. Where a piece captures leads, such as a gated guide, pass those contacts into your sales automation with the article attached. Reps then see what each lead read first.

faq_plan.q: What is the definition of a content workflow for a marketing team?
faq_plan.ref: what is a content workflow definition
faq_plan.a: Salsify's definition fits a marketing team well: a content workflow is a series of steps and responsibilities a brand needs to follow to produce and publish content. The second half of that definition matters most in practice. A stage with no named person is where a piece stalls. Put a name next to every step of your editorial workflow before you add any tooling.

faq_plan.q: How do companies automate content workflows with AI agents?
faq_plan.ref: how companies automate content workflows with ai agents
faq_plan.a: Start by giving AI agents the routing in a content workflow, and leave the writing with people. An agent reads each new brief and picks the writer by topic, then chases anything past its date. Writers and editors keep the drafting and the final edit. Emergent builds that kind of app from a plain-English prompt, and you adjust a rule by describing the new one.

faq_plan.q: What does a content creation workflow look like for a small team?
faq_plan.a: A small team's content creation workflow runs on 5 stages: brief, draft, edit, publish, and promote. Name one owner per stage, even if one person owns two stages. The promote stage is the easiest one to skip when deadlines pile up. Hand it to social media automation that posts the approved captions on a schedule.

faq_plan.q: What should content workflow software do?
faq_plan.a: Content workflow software should keep every piece's brief and due date in one place, with a named owner. It should also alert the owner when a date passes and send finished work to your CMS without copy and paste. Emergent builds that software as your own app, with no task cap and every record in a database you own.

faq_plan.q: What goes into a content production workflow?
faq_plan.a: A content production workflow covers the making of each piece up to the final checks before publishing, design work included. Strategy decides what to make and for whom. Production decides who makes it and by which date, and it is the part a board and due dates can measure.

faq_plan.q: What does content workflow management involve day to day?
faq_plan.a: Day to day, content workflow management means checking the board for pieces past their date and moving work off overloaded writers. It also means keeping sign-off from turning into the bottleneck. When a draft needs several reviewers in order, such as legal after the editor, set up a separate content approval workflow for those pieces.

plan.angle: The top 10 are DAM and CMS vendors and explainers that define the stages of a content workflow in the abstract. This page draws one article's path through a working app at a B2B software company: a brief that becomes a board item with a writer and dates, a draft 2 days late that reaches the managing editor, a finished article sent to the CMS with every field filled, and a published post that opens 3 repurposing tasks. The FAQ answers the definitions and the how-to questions searchers compare.

findings.quote: What is the definition of a content workflow for a marketing team?
findings.issue: FAQ 5 asks the definition question again after FAQ 1 ('What is a content workflow?') and lands on the same point: FAQ 1 'Each task has an owner and a due date' vs FAQ 5 'A stage with no named person is where a piece stalls.'
findings.fix: Keep FAQ 5's Salsify angle but make it answer something new for a marketing team (who owns which stage across marketing and product), not the definition again.
